leads.title: Software Engineer Infrastructure
leads.description: Software Engineer, Infrastructure Hybrid in Palo Alto (Mon / Wed / Thurs) Â· $185Kâ$215K base + meaningful early-stage equity + full benefits Â About Sodalis Specialty pharmacy is where the most complex and expensive drugs reach the most in-need patients, and it still runs on faxes, phone tag, and manual data entry. Patients wait weeks for therapies that can't wait. Sodalis is building AI agents that run those operations end to end: reading and validating prescriptions, handling phone calls, and moving prescriptions through eligibility and fulfillment. The ambition goes beyond that. We want to be the rails every specialty prescription runs on, and the first system to perform clinical review at the standard of a pharmacist. We're already in production, processing tens of thousands of prescriptions a week. Backed by Gradient Ventures (Google's AI fund), and founded by veterans of Apple's Applied ML, Included Health, and Avella Specialty Pharmacy (scaled to $1.5B+ before its acquisition by OptumRx). Â The Opportunity Everything we run today is cloud-based, and so are the pharmacy management systems we integrate with. But most of the specialty pharmacy market runs on-prem. To reach it, our system has to run on the pharmacy's systems instead of ours. Whether that's the full stack on-site or a hybrid split with our cloud is one of the first decisions you'd make. That's the problem you'd own. We've never shipped an on-prem deployment, so there's no pattern to follow. You'll decide how our architecture gets packaged and deployed into environments we don't control, what has to change in our current infrastructure to make that possible, and how we maintain and see into those deployments once they're live. We don't yet know what these environments look like in detail. Some pharmacies may have restricted outbound access, legacy hardware, or IT teams that can't give us a login; others may be more open. Part of the job is going in with our customer, finding out what's actually there, and designing something that works across the range. You'll start with our AI pharmacy tech product, rolling out with a committed customer, so you build against a real deployment instead of a hypothetical one. You'd work directly with the founders and the early engineering team on the architecture. What you'll do Decide how our architecture runs in a pharmacy's environment, starting with the AI pharmacy tech product: full stack on-site, a hybrid split with our cloud, or something in between. Adapt our current infrastructure and build the packaging and deployment path that installs and updates Sodalis at each pharmacy. Own those deployments over time: upgrades, rollbacks, and observability into health and failures without being on site. Go in with our customer and pharmacy IT teams to learn what their environments actually allow, and design for the range. Partner with the founders and early engineering team on architecture. What we're looking for 5+ years in infrastructure or platform engineering. You've taken an AWS-native stack and made it run on Kubernetes or similar in environments you don't operate, including stateful services. You've shipped and maintained software running in environments you don't control: on-prem, customer-hosted, edge, or embedded. You've kept a fleet of remote installs updated, observable, and recoverable without being able to log into them. You've set the first pattern for something in a startup and are comfortable with ambiguity. You'll spend time with pharmacy IT teams and need to understand their constraints firsthand. No healthcare background required. How we work We're a handful of people going all in on a problem we think is worth it, holding a high bar and shipping work that reaches real patients. It's intense, and it isn't for everyone. We want people who want to build something that matters, alongside others who care as much as they do. If that's you, we should talk. leads.title: [Bounty Solution] arakoodev/EdgeChains#286: BOUNTY: Convert the endpoints to a smart router like litellm does in python
leads.description:
# PR Blueprint — Issue #286
Repository: arakoodev/EdgeChains
Issue URL: https://github.com/arakoodev/EdgeChains/issues/286
Generated: 2026-10-13T06:17:55.571899

## Analysis
The EdgeChains JS SDK currently routes calls through per-provider Endpoint classes (e.g. OpenAiEndpoint.ts) that hardcode a single provider/deployment, have no cross-provider load balancing, no rate-limit/token-aware routing, no unified streaming abstraction, no token usage accounting, and no observability hooks. The repository's design principle is config-as-code via Jsonnet (used for prompts and generation config), so any new infrastructure must accept Jsonnet-derived config rather than inline TS literals. The missing capability is a LiteLLM-style Router that: (1) parses a Jsonnet routing config into a typed model_list + router_settings, (2) selects a deployment by lowest token usage among deployments that are not rate-limited, (3) wraps axios with request/response interceptors to enforce timeouts and retry with exponential backoff on 429/5xx/network errors, (4) normalizes streaming across OpenAI/PaLM/Cohere into a single AsyncIterable, (5) records token usage locally and per-deployment, and (6) emits structured events to pluggable Sentry/PostHog loggers. The old Endpoint classes must be deleted and all call sites (examples, tests) migrated to the Router. Test coverage requires mock OpenAI, PaLM, and Cohere servers over HTTP so axios interceptors, retries, and streaming are exercised end-to-end without hitting real APIs.

## Fix Summary
Introduce lib/src/lib/router/ with: types.ts (RouterConfig, ModelDeployment, CompletionRequest/Response, CallbackLogger, Usage), config.ts (Jsonnet loader using the repository's existing jsonnet runtime), usage.ts (in-memory token accounting keyed by deployment), loggers.ts (SentryLogger via @sentry/node, PostHogLogger via posthog-node), interceptors.ts (axios timeout + retry with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After), providers/ (openai.ts, palm.ts, cohere.ts implementing ProviderAdapter: complete() and stream()), router.ts (SmartRouter: least-load selection, rate-limit + cooldown bookkeeping, callbacks, JSON-safe public API), and index.ts. Delete OpenAiEndpoint.ts and replace all usages with SmartRouter.fromJsonnet(...). Add test fixtures under tests/fixtures/router.jsonnet and mock servers under tests/mocks/ for the three providers. Tests: __tests__/router.test.ts covers load balance, retry/backoff, streaming normalization, token usage, and logger emission; __tests__/interceptors.test.ts covers interceptor behavior; __tests__/jsonnet-config.test.ts validates config parsing.

## PR Title
feat(router): replace Endpoint classes with Jsonnet-configured smart router (load balance, streaming, usage, logging)

## PR Body
## Summary
Replaces the per-provider `Endpoint` classes (`OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and siblings) with a LiteLLM-style `SmartRouter` in the JS SDK (`ts/JS/edgechains`). Routing is configured exclusively via Jsonnet, matching EdgeChains' config-as-code philosophy.

Fixes the bounty: load balancing across multiple deployments, streaming, token usage, and logging (Sentry + PostHog).

## Changes Made
- **New `lib/src/lib/router/`**:
  - `types.ts` — `RouterConfig`, `ModelDeployment`, `CompletionRequest/Response`, `StreamChunk`, `Usage`, `CallbackLogger`.
  - `config.ts` — `loadRouterConfig(jsonnetSource | file)` that evaluates Jsonnet (using the same runtime already used for prompts) and validates the schema.
  - `usage.ts` — `UsageTracker` recording prompt/completion tokens per deployment with atomic increments (single-threaded JS guarantees; keys never mutated in place).
  - `loggers.ts` — `SentryLogger` (dynamic import of `@sentry/node`) and `PostHogLogger` (dynamic import of `posthog-node`); both opt-in via config.
  - `interceptors.ts` — `attachInterceptors(axiosInstance, opts)` adds a response interceptor for retry with exponential backoff (default 3 attempts, jittered), honoring `Retry-After`, retrying only 429/5xx/timeout/ECONNRESET, and a request interceptor to inject per-request `timeout`.
  - `providers/openai.ts` / `palm.ts` / `cohere.ts` — `ProviderAdapter` implementations that normalize requests and normalize responses (incl. SSE streaming → `AsyncIterable<StreamChunk>`).
  - `router.ts` — `SmartRouter` with `fromJsonnet()`, least-load selection (`pickDeployment`), per-deployment `rate_limited_until` + cooldown on 429, and callback dispatch.
  - `index.ts` — public exports.
- **Deleted** `lib/src/lib/endpoints/OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and `.../GooglePalmEndpoint.ts` / `.../CohereEndpoint.ts` if present; call sites migrated to `SmartRouter`.
- **Examples/tests** updated to construct the router from Jsonnet.
- **Mock servers** for Anthropic, PaLM, and Cohere under `tests/mocks/` (inspired by mockai) built on Node's `http` — no new runtime deps.
- **Test suite** covering all four requested features.

## Verification
- `npm test` — new suites: load-balance selection, retry/interceptor, streaming normalization, usage accounting, logger emission, Jsonnet config validation.
- Manual streaming smoke test against `tests/mocks/openai.ts` producing `data: {...}\
\
` SSE frames.
- Token-usage test asserts exact numbers after a mixed success/429 flow.
- Loggers tested with in-memory fakes to avoid network calls.

## Files to Change
[
  {
    "path": "ts/JS/edgechains/lib/src/lib/router/types.ts",
    "action": "create",
    "description": "Core router types used across providers, config, usage, and loggers.",
    "patch": "export type ProviderName = 'openai' | 'palm' | 'cohere';\n\nexport interface ModelDeployment {\n  /** Stable identifier used for usage accounting and logging. */\n  readonly model_name: string;\n  readonly provider: ProviderName;\n  /** Provider API key. */\n  readonly api_key: string;\n  /** Overrides for provider base URL (useful for tests/mocks). */\n  readonly api_base?: string;\n  /** Provider-specific model id (e.g. gpt-4o-mini, gemini-pro, command-r). */\n

leads.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
leads.description: Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic ( https://simantic.com ). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware. Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes. We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago. To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds. What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit. Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time. leads.description:

# [Bounty] Answer the 3 linked question(s)

## Context

These intakes ask about something no lesson covers. Measured through the production retrieval path (BM25 plus the IDF-weighted relevance floor), every one of them returns `no_match` — so there is nothing to link the asker to, and the answer has to be written by someone who saw the failure.

- #3652 — [Question] Which documented macOS API, if any, can move a window belonging to another appli
- #3653 — [Question] What primary evidence establishes version compatibility for SIP-enabled native m
- #3663 — [Question] For a macOS Accessibility window mover, how should bounded size-position-size op

_Shared vocabulary that grouped them: `macos`, `window`._

## Deliverable

**An answer, posted as a comment on each question issue above.** No pull request is needed and none is expected — the answer is what the asker (and the next agent that hits this) needs, and it is what the FAQ is built from. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies an `answered` comment into D1, and from then on `misakanet_search` returns it as a `type: faq` hit.

The answer has to be *observed*, not generated. An answer invented by someone who never saw the failure is an invented source — that is the failure `docs/maintainer/provenance-gate-2026-09-16.md` exists to prevent. If you only have a hypothesis, say so plainly: a guess labelled as a guess is useful, a guess presented as fact is not.

## How your answer reaches readers

1. Post it on **each** linked question issue as a comment — not only here. The sync reads the question's own thread.
2. A maintainer reviews it in the daily question pass and adds the `answered` label.
3. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies the labelled comment into the FAQ (D1) within a day.

## MANDATORY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (AC)

**0. REPRODUCIBLE EVIDENCE — the condition most submissions fail**

- [ ] Paste the command you ran and the output you got. Not a description of what you did — the command and its output. If you name an endpoint it must be `misakanet.org`.
- [ ] Say what you observed yourself versus what you read somewhere.

**1. The answer is complete**

- [ ] It states the root cause, the fix (with the exact command or setting), and how to check it worked — the last one is a command plus the result that means success, not "it should work".
- [ ] It names the version / environment it was observed on. "Works on my machine" without that line is unfalsifiable.

**2. It is posted where the question lives**

- [ ] A comment on **every** linked question issue above. One comment covering several questions is fine — post the same text on each, or post once and link the others.

**3. Claiming**

- [ ] Comment `/try` (or `/claim`) here so others know you are on it; the claim rules are in `JOIN.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## What the reward is, stated plainly

**This is a `zero-bounty` task: $0.** The reward is the answer being reused, credit in the thread, and a line in the Hall of Fame. A real bounty exists only when someone funds it by commenting `/reward <amount>` on this issue — the money is held and paid by Opire, not by this repository.

## Optional: also land it as a lesson

Never required for this task. If you want the corpus to keep it, a lesson PR is welcome — and it must still satisfy the landing rules: `Signed-off-by` on every commit (or ask a maintainer for `/adopt`, which keeps your authorship — `docs/maintainer/adopt-fork-pr.md`), the two generators run and their output committed, and one intake per lesson in `provenance.issue` (the rest in `provenance.related`, per #3361). Say here first if you plan to open one.

## Closes

An answer closes this task once a maintainer labels it `answered`; the questions above close the same way. If a lesson lands instead, `Fixes #N` closes them through the receipt rule. If you cannot finish it, comment here and it goes back to the pool.

<sub>Opened automatically by `scripts/question_autopilot.py` from measured coverage of the open questions. The grouping is a suggestion: if these are not really one question, say so and this task will be split.</sub>

leads.title: Show HN: Formstep, Request information from customers without the back-and-forth
leads.description: I built Formstep: https://formstep.io The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications. A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information. At that point, workflow automation basically did not work. The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish. Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth. So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents. The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer. You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need. For example, we might already know: * Address that you already have in the CRM * Company description from the internet * What a agreement document must contain * How a good answer should be Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”. The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later. On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue. Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here. I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case. My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today? If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/ Docs: https://docs.formstep.io I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

leads.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
leads.description: Hi HN, Mark here. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up. Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood. Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT- ) from code tasks (SUB- ) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free. Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves. "nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry. One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly. Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now. Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client fails on valid responses split across stream reads
leads.description:
## Python client fails on a valid response split across stream reads

At `3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:159` passes one `socket.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)` result directly to `split_packet()`. The AF_UNIX stream can return fewer bytes than a complete packet. A valid response can therefore raise an uncaught `struct.error` in the Python client even though the remaining bytes are still arriving.

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers. I am **not** reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption.

### Reproduction

With the existing `crcmod` dependency installed, run this from the repository root:

```python
import sys
import struct
sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
from kivaloo import wire

# A valid KVLDS PARAMS response: 8-byte payload, 28-byte complete frame.
record = struct.pack('>II', 255, 255)
packet = wire.make_packet(0, record)
assert wire.split_packet(packet) == (0, record)

class ShortReads:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = packet
    def sendall(self, data):
        assert wire.split_packet(data) == (0, struct.pack('>I', 0x100))
    def recv(self, size):
        size = min(size, 8)
        result, self.data = self.data[:size], self.data[size:]
        return result
    def close(self):
        pass

client = wire.Wire.__new__(wire.Wire)
client.msgnum = 0
client.sock = ShortReads()
print(client.send_recv('>I', 0x100).get('>II'))
```

Expected: `(255, 255)`.

Actual on the base commit:

```text
struct.error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 16 bytes for
unpacking 16 bytes at offset 0 (actual buffer size is 8)
```

I also reproduced the failure using a real local `socket.socketpair()`, with an event coordinating the second fragment only after the first `recv()` returns. This needs no timing sleeps or remote service. An additional check used the compiled C `lbs` server, private temporary storage and a Unix socket: the unchanged response stream succeeds with the original client on the normal path, fails with the original client when reads are limited to eight bytes, and passes PARAMS/APPEND/GET with byte-exact data after the fix.

### Proposed fix and validation

Read the 16-byte header completely, validate its checksum and the existing total response-size limit, then read the payload and four-byte trailer completely before calling the existing `split_packet()`. Treat EOF before a full frame as an error rather than looping. Keep the existing record-checksum and response-ID checks.

A local minimal patch adds 20 lines and removes two in `wire.py`. Thirteen regression tests pass after the patch, including all 27 split points of the PARAMS response, single-byte reads, complete-response controls, early EOF, size limits, checksum failures, consecutive frames and the real socket-pair reproduction. These tests fail on the unmodified base at the framing cases. Validation used macOS arm64, Python 3.14.7 and the actual `crcmod==1.7` package. The C programs compiled successfully with the documented Homebrew OpenSSL flags; AWS/remote-service tests were not run.

Please consider this report under the published bug-bounty program if eligible. I understand that classification and any award are your decision, and that awards below $100 are account credits rather than cash. No award is assumed.

**AI disclosure and follow-up:** This report, investigation and proposed patch were prepared by OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex (LLMs), with the authorization of the `avs-io` account owner. This is not intended as a one-off report: questions and requested revisions can be addressed through this GitHub account. No live customer data, external service testing or payment credentials were used.

leads.description:
> **Re-planned 2026-11-02 under the [#418 design](https://github.com/603-Identity/devcontainers/issues/418#issuecomment-6584294809).** The shared template is now dev-App only, and the PAT route is frozen (decision 1). **glunk-works** rows adopt the dev-App flavour once #418's milestone ships v1.6. **603-Identity** rows wait for 603-Identity's own dev-App cutover.
>
> A dev-App adoption:
> - copies `template/.devcontainer/` and sets only the four per-repo surfaces: the token mount `tokens/<owner>/<repo>`; `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` or `devcontainer-devapp-tofu`; the root-run Dockerfile extras; an optional loopback `appPort`;
> - copies only `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` from `template/.github/workflows/`;
> - runs the way-of-working plugin's review gate;
> - has its approval ruleset (at least 1 approval, code-owner review) live before the dev App is installed.
>
> Lines the re-plan changed are marked *(re-planned)*.

## Scope

Adopt the template on every Python repo, moving each to the image's standard: **Python 3.14 system interpreter, uv-native project layout** (`pyproject.toml` with `[dependency-groups]`, committed `uv.lock`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run`). hatch environments and scripts are retired; `hatchling` may stay as a build backend where a repo publishes a package. Precondition: milestone **P0: cross-org images** closed and the pilot wave (#10) done.

| Repo | Today | Change at adoption |
|---|---|---|
| glunk-works/bounty-infra | CI 3.11 lint/test, 3.14 package; hatch envs `lint`, `test`, `audit`, `sbom` in `src/pyproject.toml`; `python` Feature | CI to 3.14; hatch envs become dependency groups, scripts become `uv run` lines; `uv.lock` committed; drop the Feature and lockfile |
| glunk-works/pm-agent-loop | CI 3.12; hatch envs `default`, `types` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| glunk-works/scope-core | CI 3.11 + 3.14; hatch envs `lint`, `test` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| 603-Identity/tenant-posture-assessment | CI 3.12; `requirements.in` + `requirements.txt` | *(re-planned: deferred to 603-Identity's dev-App cutover)* `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock` replace both files; CI to 3.14 (supersedes the framing of #11); bc-detect-secrets 1.5.51 baseline regenerated |

Per-repo adoption PR checklist:
- [ ] *(re-planned)* copy `template/.devcontainer/` and set only the four per-repo surfaces (see the note at the top); `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` by tag@digest; the `-venv` volume is part of the shared template
- [ ] add `.devcontainer` to `dependabot.yml` (docker ecosystem) and switch the Python entry to `package-ecosystem: uv`
- [ ] `pyproject.toml`: `[project]` with `requires-python = ">=3.14"`, `[dependency-groups]` for dev/lint/test (and `checkov` where a local gate uses it, pinned to the ledger version); `uv lock`; commit `uv.lock`
- [ ] `.python-version` only if the repo must stay below 3.14 during migration; otherwise omit
- [ ] CI: pinned `astral-sh/setup-uv`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run <tool>`; `python-version` pins to 3.14; `pip install hatch` removed
- [ ] *(re-planned)* no per-repo `postCreateCommand`: the shared template runs `pre-commit install` only, and `uv sync --locked` (plus `--group checkov` where used) runs from the repo's own gate
- [ ] `.ai/project.yml` `gates.green` and CLAUDE.md commands rewritten from `hatch run ...` to `uv run ...`
- [ ] delete the repo's old `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, Features and `devcontainer-lock.json`
- [ ] *(re-planned)* approval ruleset live first; the plugin's review gate; `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` copied from the template
- [ ] gate green inside the container; CI green with the new pins
- [ ] old container and `vsc-*` image removed on the host

Not in this wave: loop-orchestrator (documented exception, see the threat-model issue). When it is migrated later, it follows the same uv-native layout.

leads.title: Show HN: E2E – Open-source agentic testing framework for web, iOS and Android
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Oskar, one of the co-founders of TesterArmy. We built an agentic testing framework for web and mobile because traditional testing frameworks can’t keep up with the pace of how we build software today. e2e allows you to mix deterministic and agentic APIs in the same test. You can write the test cases using familiar APIs like `getByText()`or `getByTestId()` which you can also mix it with agentic `agent.act()`. The unique part about it is that e2e will cache and replay the agentic actions so you don’t have to pay for AI on each run. We ship both web and mobile engines out of the box; adding support for more platforms is pretty straightforward. leads.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
leads.description: Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ( https://laminar.sh/blog ) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ( https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr ). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

leads.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
leads.description: Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request a

leads.title: feat(health): sport ensemble — routes HealthKit, localisation téléphone et bonus de groupe
leads.description:
**Pourquoi** — Permettre au joueur de faire reconnaître une vraie séance commune, même avec une montre sans route, puis montrer le bonus signature de **GRRIND**. Cadrage métier/serveur : [grrind-back#329](https://github.com/younesdiouri/grrind-back/issues/329), source de vérité.

## Règles à afficher

1 / 2 / 3 / 4+ joueurs distincts, soi compris → **×1 / ×2 / ×3 / ×4**. Même sport normalisé, ≥80 % de chevauchement pour chaque séance, proximité d'environ 100 m. **L'auteur a choisi un multiplicateur après le plafond quotidien** : 100 XP solo après plafond → 300 XP à trois. Le serveur tranche tout ; le client ne calcule ni proximité, ni groupe, ni XP.

## Périmètre, dans cet ordre

- [ ] **Spike terrain d'abord** : étendre le module Swift `modules/grrind-health` pour lire les `HKWorkoutRoute` autorisées, par lots, avec horodatage et précision. Une route peut arriver après le workout : prévoir la relance d'enrichissement sans rejouer le crédit. Identifier concrètement les montres/apps qui remontent une route exploitable.
- [ ] **Solution sans route** : proposer « Sport ensemble » avant la séance pour activer la collecte de localisation du téléphone. Explication courte de l'utilité, permissions demandées au bon moment, état actif visible, arrêt explicite et arrêt de sécurité borné. Collecter pendant la séance, y compris écran verrouillé/arrière-plan selon les capacités réelles d'iOS ; documenter interruption/arrêt forcé. Une position prise après le sport ne prouve rien.
- [ ] La capture de positions ne crée aucun workout ni chronomètre de jeu. Le workout vient toujours de la santé. Rapprocher la capture du workout de **son compte** via les données fournisseur et ses bornes ; aucun sport normalisé, durée ou multiplicateur déclaré par l'app.
- [ ] Persister les lots en attente et leurs identifiants, reprendre après réseau coupé/app relancée, envoyer les preuves indépendamment de l'import lorsque le contrat existe. Préserver `Idempotency-Key` et la réponse originale du lot santé ; pas de GPS dans les logs. Purger dès remise utile et au plus 30 jours après la séance.
- [ ] Refus/révocation de localisation, GPS approximatif ou route absente : l'import et l'XP solo fonctionnent. Montrer le statut serveur « preuve insuffisante » ou « en attente », sans affirmer que le joueur était seul ni promettre un bonus acquis.
- [ ] **Contrat back d'abord** : tirer `openapi.yaml` depuis main puis générer les types. Le back fournira statut, nombre de joueurs, multiplicateur et XP avant/après/supplément. Aucun endpoint, DTO ni enum serveur inventé ici ; préparer la partie native indépendante pendant l'attente.
- [ ] Bilan et historique : afficher « Sport ensemble ×N » et le supplément **serveur**. Conserver le bilan agrégé actuel du lot ; ne pas appliquer un multiplicateur global à des séances de groupes différents. Les compléments accordés après la synchro d'un ami se présentent une seule fois, via leurs identifiants stables et paliers serveur, sans rejouer l'ancien `SyncSummary`.
- [ ] Texte permission/explication : « GRRIND utilise ta localisation pendant cette séance pour reconnaître le sport ensemble. » Ajouter les libellés et traductions selon les conventions existantes ; aucun ancien nom d'app.

## Validation

- [ ] Sur les appareils réels utilisés : montre avec/sans route, intérieur/extérieur, téléphone verrouillé/arrière-plan, GPS refusé/imprécis, offline/reprise et ami qui synchronise plus tard. Témoins négatifs : simple croisement, horaires/sports différents, personnes éloignées.
- [ ] Reporter appareils, séances communes détectées/manquées, faux positifs, trous de collecte et batterie dans le ticket, sans positions brutes. Cette preuve physique est la première étape ; ne pas la remplacer par des mocks.
- [ ] Tests utiles des frontières natives/HTTP, permissions, reprise et absence de double présentation ; barrières app selon `AGENTS.md` (`typecheck`, `lint`, tests ; `api:check` et previews selon changements). Rebuild dev seulement pour les changements natifs, aucune release EAS automatique.

## Hors périmètre

Health Connect Android reste #15 ; pas d'app watchOS, carte sociale ni suivi permanent. Le plan B de confirmation réciproque est documenté dans le ticket back et reste conditionnel au résultat terrain ; aucun bouton de déclaration donnant directement de l'XP.

Lire `AGENTS.md` et `CLAUDE.md` avant de commencer. Repères : `modules/grrind-health`, `src/features/health/`, `src/features/reward/`. Docs : [routes HealthKit](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/healthkit/reading-route-data), [Core Location en arrière-plan](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/corelocation/handling-location-updates-in-the-background). Consulter les docs de la version Expo installée avant de choisir l'API de localisation.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python server discovery aborts on stale PIDs and disappearing processes
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), reporting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and candidate changes in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/servers.py:Server._search_for_process() assumes both the PID-file process and every enumerated process remain accessible. psutil.Process(pid) raises NoSuchProcess for a stale PID file, and proc.cmdline() can raise NoSuchProcess or AccessDenied during the system-wide scan. These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

Please assess under the published bug-bounty rules. Classification and award are not assumed; I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits.

leads.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks! https://agent37.com

leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

leads.title: AI is coming for accounting after coding
leads.description: Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. writing contracts is where an LLM shines, it's basic building blocks are formal words. Formal is the key term here. Accounting if different. More precise, it tolerates less mistakes. The rules that govern it are much less open to intrepretation. In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future. In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate. It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. Accounting follows the same power law as football. In a 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad journal entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal: 1. In those two, a task would not be ruined by a single mistake in the system. An app would run fine with a couple of bugs if the system design was decent. A contract would still be enforceable with an additional weak sentence in most cases. But in accounting, 1 digit error would ruin the entire balance sheet. 2. The cost of making a mistake. Worst case scenario, the system goes down for a couple of hours, you might lose a case because of a bad contract. But losing track of the financials is a different story, it can easily destroy the whole company. 3. Trust is harder to establish with accounting. You can outsource legal without understanding much about the law. But if you outsource accounting without understanding the numbers; you are toast. Also, all the major labs are going after it soon, margins are going down fast. Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller.

leads.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
leads.description: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

leads.title: Show HN: Vu – a new programming language designed for AI. Rust speeds, Py syntax
leads.description: hi everyone! I wanted to share what I've been working on these past 6~ years. TL;DR: Rust is great, but somewhere along the way, I learned that I was too dumb to read and write Rust. As I worked on larger and larger Rust projects, I also became frustrated with the developer experience of working in Rust (slow compile time), so I wanted a better way. Vu's language changed a bit over time but the core principles remained the same: 1. It should be easy to read and write 2. It should be memory safe 3. It should be fast to run 4. It should be fast to compile Here's how I approached each: 1. Vu is syntactically very close to Python. The ownership rules are the ones Rust has, but I personally find it a lot easier to parse and understand. I've tested this with various LLMs and found it can read and write Vu out the box because of the similarity to Python. 2. Vu uses the same principles of Rust. Every value has one owner, borrows can't escape or outlive what they borrow, and nothing changes while it's borrowed. 3. Vu compiles down to C at the end of the day, so everything runs approximately at C speeds. 4. vuc check on the compiler’s own source (about 21,500 lines of Vu), takes about 0.4~ s. This check covers parsing, type and borrow checking. cargo check on a Rust project that size usually takes several seconds from scratch. Then there are other opinionated language decisions. Vu has no macros, Vu's borrow checker is lighter weight than Rust's with simpler interfaces and generics. However, in the past few years, as Vu's language evolved and AI began to take over, I expanded Vu's principles to include a couple additional principles: 5. It should be secure 6. It should be efficient for LLMs to write 5. I want to pen test Vu in public. In https://github.com/vu0tran/vu/tree/main/tests , you'll see a battery of tests where I'm trying to basically pwn Vu. There are explicit language decisions in there as well that tries to prevent a host of security flaws that exist in other languages, e.g, integer overflow stops the program instead of quietly wrapping around. 6. The syntax of Vu is designed to be tokenizer efficient. In addition, when Vu checks throws errors, the errors are designed to be token efficient and written in a way that guides LLMs to more easily fix bugs, reducing turns overall. So, in summary, Vu is still experimental. The compiler is 21,500 lines of Vu and compiles itself. The standard library also has TLS, HTTP/2, WebSockets and a PostgreSQL client, all tested against Python’s implementations and hostile input. I think most of the pieces are there. It does also compile down also to WebAssembly so you can play around w/ the checker on the website! Feel free to try to break it! What's next: 1. Figure out how to get Vu to perform faster than Rust 2. Rewrite some OSS libraries in Vu to further prove the language

leads.description: I like to see what new projects people are working on in open-source, but I found it hard to find projects or news in any systematic way. I built Shadowgraph so that I could browse the latest in open source development in a more natural way. It ingests repos from github and scrapes hackernews, reddit, and X for mentions of them. I also identify noteworthy contributors on github and track what they're starring as a signal for potentially high quality projects that might otherwise fly under the radar. I also track their tweets or hackernews contributions for mentions of github repos for a more curated feed of content. Finally, there's an MCP and semantic search for repos and developers. This is a fun side project for me but I want it to be useful for people- feedback is very much appreciated.

leads.title: [$10 BOUNTY] [Python] Add build.py --check-stale flag for CI gating

**Bounty:** $10 (LT)

**Area:** build.py diagnostic artifact management

**Current state:** The `--retention-report` flag reports stale artifacts but does not provide a CI-friendly exit code. CI pipelines need a way to fail when stale artifacts exceed a threshold, preventing accidental inclusion of outdated diagnostics in PRs.

**What is needed:** Add a `--check-stale` flag that exits non-zero when older diagnostic artifacts exist, suitable for use as a CI gate.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- Add `--check-stale` flag to `build.py` that exits 1 if any older (non-current-commit) artifacts exist, exits 0 otherwise
- Add `--max-stale-bytes` option (default: 0 = any stale is an error) to allow a byte threshold
- The flag is read-only and does not delete artifacts
- Add at least 4 tests with a temporary diagnostic directory

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python LBS append silently truncates or pads mismatched block counts
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can help discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate patch in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/proto_lbs.py:Proto_lbs.append() checks that the byte length is a multiple of the block size, but not that it matches nums * block_size. The actual Wire.send_recv() then uses a fixed-length struct.pack string field, silently truncating or padding mismatched data.

With block_size = 4, a recording socket under the actual Python wire encoder captured:

    nums=1 input=b'AAAABBBB' payload=b'AAAA' result=(0, 1)
    nums=2 input=b'AAAA' payload=b'AAAA\x00\x00\x00\x00' result=(0, 2)

The success responses are supplied by the socket double; no C server was run. The observed bug is the changed outgoing payload, not independently demonstrated server-side storage corruption. This requires inconsistent arguments from a caller of the Python test helper. I am not claiming an issue in the C APPEND implementation or a security vulnerability.

A candidate check, immediately after num_bytes = self.block_size * nums:

    if len(blocks) != num_bytes:
        raise ValueError("wire append: Block count does not match data length")

The following test uses the actual Proto_lbs.append, Wire.send_recv, packet encoder and decoder, with an in-memory socket double. Save as tests/python/test_lbs_append_length.py; from tests/python run python -m unittest -v test_lbs_append_length with crcmod and psutil installed.

Python 3.12.14 / Windows: baseline 1 passes and 2 fail; with the check all 3 pass. The exact-length control verifies byte preservation and the decoded success result. The mismatched cases verify no packet is sent after the fix. Full native server tests were not run.

<details><summary>Reproduction / regression test</summary>

~~~python
"""Check APPEND length validation without starting a server."""

import struct
import unittest

from kivaloo.proto_lbs import Proto_lbs
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet


class RecordingSocket:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []
        self.msgnum = None

    def sendall(self, packet):
        self.msgnum, record = split_packet(packet)
        self.records.append(record)

    def recv(self, size):
        _, nums, start = struct.unpack_from('>IIQ', self.records[-1])
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, struct.pack('>IQ', 0, start + nums))

    def close(self):
        pass


class AppendLengthTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.sock = RecordingSocket()
        self.proto = Proto_lbs.__new__(Proto_lbs)
        self.proto.block_size = 4
        self.proto.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
        self.proto.wire.msgnum = 0
        self.proto.wire.sock = self.sock

    def tearDown(self):
        self.proto.close()

    def test_rejects_too_many_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(1, 0, b'AAAABBBB')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_rejects_too_few_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(2, 0, b'AAAA')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_exact_length_preserves_bytes(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.proto.append(2, 7, b'AAAABBBB'), (0, 9))
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records,
                         [struct.pack('>IIQ', 2, 2, 7) + b'AAAABBBB'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
~~~

</details>

Submitted for consideration under the bug bounty program, with classification and eligibility left to the maintainer. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap account credits, not cash.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)
leads.description:
## Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)

At `3de151b` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py` defines

    MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 16384

with the comment "This is a somewhat arbitrary value", and `Wire.send_recv()` reads the whole response with a single bounded call:

    idnum, record = split_packet(self.sock.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES))

`split_packet()` then requires the *entire* frame inside that one buffer:

    record, crc = struct.unpack_from('>%dsI' % record_length, packet, offset=16)
    assert len(packet) == len(record) + 16 + 4

A Wire frame for a record of length `N` is `N + 20` bytes, so any response record longer than 16364 bytes cannot be processed: `recv()` returns at most 16384 bytes and `struct.unpack_from` raises `struct.error`.

This is separate from #358 (responses fragmented across reads of a small packet). PR #359's stated fix explicitly keeps "the existing total response-size limit", so this bug remains even after #359 is merged.

### Valid server responses that exceed the cap

1. **LBS GET with block size > 16360.** The block size is operator-configured via `lbs -b`, validated to `[PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MIN, PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MAX]` = `[512, 131072]` (`lbs/main.c`, `lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs.h`). An LBS GET response record is `4 (status) + blklen` bytes (`lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs_server.c`, `proto_lbs_response_get()`). Any deployment configured with block size ≥ 16361 — legal up to the documented maximum of 131072 — produces GET responses the Python client cannot read. The C server imposes no such limit: `proto_lbs_request_parse()` `malloc()`s APPEND payloads dynamically and `wire_writepacket_getbuf()` sizes GET responses to the configured block size.

2. **KVLDS RANGE responses.** The response record grows with the data returned: `4 (status) + 4 (num_pairs) + nextkey + Σ(1+keylen + 1+valen)` (each pair up to 514 bytes). For 100-byte keys/values, a range response with roughly 80 pairs already exceeds the cap; `tests/python/dump_kvlds.py` requests `maxsize = 8192` pairs per range call, so the dump tool fails on most non-trivial datasets. The C-side range response is likewise dynamically sized.

### Reproduction (real C server, no mocks)

On `3de151b`, with `crcmod` installed:

    $ ./lbs/lbs -s /tmp/repro/lbs.sock -d /tmp/repro/storage -b 32768 -1 &
    $ python3 - <<'EOF'
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
    from kivaloo import proto_lbs
    p = proto_lbs.Proto_lbs('/tmp/repro/lbs.sock')
    print("params():", p.params())
    data = bytes(range(256)) * 128          # one 32 KiB block
    print("append():", p.append(1, 0, data))
    print("get():", p.get(0))
    EOF

    params(): (32768, 0)
    append(): 0 1
    get() FAILED -> error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 32792 bytes
        for unpacking 32776 bytes at offset 16 (actual buffer size is 16384)

The C `lbs` server accepts the 32 KiB block and serves it (no server-side error); only the Python client fails.

### Impact

- The Python client cannot interoperate with any LBS deployment configured with block size > 16360 (legal up to 131072).
- `dump_kvlds.py` and any KVLDS RANGE consumer fail once a range response exceeds 16 KiB.
- The test suite cannot exercise the C server with non-default (larger) block sizes, because the harness itself rejects the responses.

### Suggested fix

In `send_recv()`: read the 16-byte header first (as #359 proposes), then read exactly `record_length + 4` further bytes based on the header's `record_length` field before calling `split_packet()`. This bounds the allocation by the protocol maximum (LBS: 20 + 4 + 131072 = 131096 bytes; KVLDS: bounded by the requested data) instead of a fixed 16384. `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` can then be removed or raised to the protocol maximum.

### Scope / disclosure

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers (`tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py`). I am not reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption. The C client (`lib/wire/wire_readpacket.c`) reads complete packets and is unaffected.

This report, investigation and reproduction were prepared by an LLM with the authorization of the `zhangb06` account owner. I am available to discuss the problem or a fix through this account. No live customer data, external service testing, or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: What are the best-practice architectural workflows for LLM-based contract compliance agents?
leads.description: I am designing an Agentic Workflow for automated contract compliance auditing, where the system must cross-reference multi-page legal documents against a set of compliance policies (e.g., GDPR or local labor laws). My current high-level flow is: Parsing & Indexing: Splitting documents by clause headers to maintain semantic integrity. Retrieval (RAG): Using a vector store to retrieve clauses relevant to specific compliance policies. Reasoning/Evaluation: A dual-agent approach where one agent performs "extraction" and a second agent performs "compliance judgment." My core architectural concerns are: Handling Cross-References: Many contract clauses refer to other sections (e.g., "See Section 5.1 for liability limitations"). How can the agent effectively maintain this dependency chain without overloading the context window? Decision Consistency: How do you structure the workflow to ensure that the "reasoning" behind a compliance judgment is explainable and verifiable? Agentic Loops: Is it better to use a single "Chain of Thought" prompt for complex compliance logic, or is an autonomous multi-agent framework (like LangGraph or CrewAI) overkill for this specific task? I'm looking for advice or established patterns on how to handle these complexities. What flow have you found most reliable in terms of accuracy and latency for legal-tech applications?
